ideas.title: I Fixed the Darvas Box: 74.2% Win Rate Over 33 Years
ideas.name: Mechanical Darvas box breakout on SPY (12-day high, capped chase, volume filter)
ideas.entry: Signal day: close is above the highest high of the previous 12 trading days, but by no more than 0.75% of that level, and volume is above its 15-day average (whether the average includes the signal day is unstated). Buy at the next open.
ideas.exit: When the close is above the previous day's high, sell at the next open. No stop mentioned.
ideas.filters: none by design (the video says it uses no RSI, no 200-day average, no seasonality)
ideas.claimed_results: SPY 1993 to 2026 (33 years). 279 trades, 74.2% winners, average trade +0.34%, profit factor 3.08, average hold about 3 trading days. Profit factor by era: 2.70 (1993-2004), 2.78 (2005-2015), 3.94 (2016-2026). Lookback sweep profit factors: 11d 2.75, 13d 2.97, 16d 2.84, 18d 2.71, 20d 2.80; 12d is the best at 3.08. Costs not mentioned. My arithmetic, not stated: 279 trades x 3 days over about 8,300 sessions is roughly 10% exposure.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: none. It is a breakout, unlike everything tested so far. It shares the close-above-yesterday's-high exit with the RSI(2) sweep.
ideas.red_flags: The 0.75% chase cap and 15-day volume filter look tuned and were not swept; only the lookback was. No null comparison (same exit from random entries, or a plain 12-day-high entry without the extras). That exit lifts win rate and profit factor structurally because losers have no stop. Costs not shown. Sits oddly beside this channel's own finding that 252-day-high closes underperform over 20 days (A-32); horizon and exit differ. Promotional framing in the title.
ideas.why_priority: Complete rules, free daily data, a checkable trade count and profit factor, and the only genuinely different entry type in the folder.

ideas.title: Which Nasdaq Stocks Work Best With Williams %R? We Tested 100
ideas.name: Williams %R(2) oversold dip-buy across 101 Nasdaq-100 stocks
ideas.entry: Williams %R with a 2-day lookback closes below -90. Buy at the signal close (headline test) or at the next open (variant).
ideas.exit: Close above the prior day's high, or Williams %R rises above -30, whichever comes first.
ideas.claimed_results: Test period unstated. 95 of 101 stocks had profit factor above 1; 58 above 1.5; 26 above 2. Median profit factor 1.57 at the close, 1.47 at the next open; only 23 stocks improved with next-open entry. Apple first: 165 trades, 72.1% winners, average trade +1.19%, profit factor 3.08 (3.36 at next open). Microsoft just over 3.0, Monolithic Power 2.94, Meta 2.71, KLA 2.70, Marvell 2.49 on 216 trades. Weak: Palantir, Fang, Airbnb, CrowdStrike.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Same family as the RSI(2) sweep, but across single stocks rather than an index, with a different oscillator.
ideas.red_flags: Survivorship and selection bias, stated by the video: today's constituents tested backwards. The 101 stocks share market days, so 95 of 101 is not 95 independent confirmations. Costs and period unstated. Short-history names have few trades. We would need a current constituent list; point-in-time membership is not free. Headline names are the best of 101, so the median is the number to trust.
ideas.why_priority: Breadth across 101 names is a far stronger luck test than another SPY run, rules are complete, and the median profit factor is a clear number to check.

ideas.title: Improve Your Trading With Kaufman Indicators - Perry Kaufman And Kevin Davey
ideas.name: Efficiency ratio ranking of markets (also stated in fI3IWoTORUo)
ideas.markets: any basket of markets; Kaufman names interest-rate markets and stock-index markets as the two ends of the ranking
ideas.entry: No trade rule. Compute the efficiency ratio over a short window (Kaufman suggests about 10 bars, the shortest that spreads the values out), rank all markets, then use trend systems on the high end and mean-reversion systems on the low end. As spoken the formula is the sum of absolute bar-to-bar moves versus the net distance, but he also says a higher value means more trending, which is inconsistent; the standard form is net change divided by total path, between 0 and 1, high = trending.
ideas.exit: unstated (selection filter, not a trade rule)
ideas.filters: market selection by ER rank; no fixed threshold, ranking is relative
ideas.claimed_results: No performance numbers. Checkable claims: interest-rate markets come out as the most trending and stock-index markets as the least trending, and Kaufman says that if your ranking does not show this you have computed it wrongly. ER is said to be fractal: markets high on daily bars are also high on 60-minute bars. In Davey's 44-market test the filtered trend system had a negative average trade over all markets; Kaufman says choosing high-ER markets would have removed that problem (asserted, not shown).
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Feeds P-0084 (28-market trend portfolio, market selection) and supports the RSI(5) index-ETF book (index markets are the least trending, so mean reversion fits). Not tested before.
ideas.red_flags: Formula is garbled in the transcript, so pre-register the standard definition. The sanity check is circular as a validation. Kaufman is promoting his own signals site and the masterclass. Window choice is described as important but only 10 is suggested.
ideas.why_priority: Free daily data, near-complete rule, a stated claim we can check in an hour, and the result directly informs the queued trend portfolio and the running RSI(5) book.

ideas.name: RSI-PCA walk-forward return predictor
ideas.markets: BTCUSDT hourly close only (BTCUSDT3600.csv). The in-sample file uses data before 2020-01-01; the walk-forward is scored from 2020 onward
ideas.entry: Wilder RSI (pandas_ta) for every period 2..24 (23 features), centred by the training-window mean, projected on the first 3 eigenvectors of their covariance, then least squares (no intercept) onto the next-6-bar log return. Long signal when the prediction exceeds the 99th percentile of the training window's own predictions, short signal below the 1st percentile. The position is the 6-bar rolling mean of the raw +1/-1/0 signal, so every signal is held 6 bars and overlapping signals stack into a fractional position
ideas.exit: No explicit exit: each signal drops out of the rolling mean after 6 bars
ideas.parameters: RSI periods 2..24; n_components 3; lookahead 6; rolling train window 2 years of bars (24*365*2); retrain every 1 year of bars; tail thresholds 1% and 99%. Nothing is optimised in the main run, but a commented heatmap sweeps lookahead 1..24 x components 1..6 on the walk-forward profit factor, and the 3 and 6 used look picked from it
ideas.claimed_results: none (README only links a video; the plot label says 'RSI-PSA 3-6 Model')
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Partial: built on RSI like the RSI(5) tests, but a multi-period model rather than a threshold rule. Not tested before
ideas.red_flags: Eigenvector bug: scipy eigh returns eigenvectors as columns, but the code uses evecs[j], a row, at RSI-PCA.txt lines 39, 114, 189 and 241, so the 'principal components' are not the real PCs (still a rotation applied consistently, so not look-ahead). No look-ahead otherwise: walkforward.py line 232 drops the last 6 training rows so every label is known at the fit date. Fills at the signal bar's close (return close i to i+1), no costs. 6-bar targets overlap heavily so the effective sample is small. On daily bars a 2-year window puts only about 5 points in each 1% tail, so train much longer (8+ years on ETFs)
ideas.why_priority: Builds on the only edge that survived (RSI dip-buying), has complete walk-forward code, and asks whether a multi-period RSI model beats the single RSI(5) rule

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Fed decision day return and pre-Fed drift
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures as stated (daily proxies would be QQQ, SPY, ^NDX, ^GSPC)
ideas.entry: unstated (the drift is described as stocks rising over the 24 hours before the decision; no trade rule given)
ideas.exit: unstated
ideas.filters: Fed decision dates only (52 decisions since 2020)
ideas.claimed_results: Nasdaq averaged +0.36 percent on Fed decision days; about one in eight random samples of ordinary days matched that. The pre-Fed drift over the 24 hours before the decision was visible but about one in ten random samples matched it, and it lost money in 2025 and 2026. Author's verdict: not a proven edge.
ideas.red_flags: Only 52 events. Return basis (close to close, open to close) is unstated. The announcement is at 2pm, so a daily bar cannot isolate the 24 hours before it exactly; a daily proxy blurs the claim. Fed dates from the Fed site are free, but we must write the calendar ourselves.
ideas.why_priority: A stated number with a random-sample comparison, checkable on decades of free daily ETF history instead of his 52 events; pre-register the definition before running.

ideas.title: I Backtested 10 Oscillators on SPY for 33 Years
ideas.name: Williams %R(7) below -95 on SPY, frozen development and holdout (also FXYI7n6XJlk)
ideas.entry: Williams %R over 7 days is below -95 at the daily close; buy SPY at the next open; one position at a time.
ideas.exit: SPY closes above the previous day's high; exit at the next open. The video also tests fixed 1, 3 and 5 day exits.
ideas.claimed_results: 1993 to 2026: 288 trades, profit factor 2.61, average trade 0.82%, 76.4% winners, max drawdown 12.1%. Profit factor by era: 3.01 (1993-2003), 2.51 (2004-2014), 2.28 (2015-2026). Second video: 42 parameter combinations, settings chosen on 1993-2015 and locked, untouched 2016-2026 holdout profit factor 2.08 (RSI 1.12, stochastic 1.75). Median profit factor across the 42 development combinations 2.02. Scorecard 92 out of 100 against 75 and 33. Costs excluded.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Same entry style and the same close-above-yesterday's-high exit as the RSI(2) sweep, which was not among the P-0082 survivors. Likely trades many of the same days as the RSI(5) book.
ideas.red_flags: Winner of a 10-way contest and of a 42-combination grid, so selection bias. The holdout is not clean: the three oscillators compared in the second video were shortlisted from the earlier full-sample ranking. Williams %R(7) below -95 is just the close sitting in the bottom 5% of the 7-day range, a fast stochastic. Costs excluded. Ten oscillators with one exit are largely one trade, not ten edges.
ideas.why_priority: Complete rules and a stated holdout number to check, but it is a close relative of something we already tested, so run it with the permutation test and measure entry-day overlap with the RSI(5) book.

ideas.title: This Stochastic Strategy Won 77.7% Over 33 Years
ideas.name: 7-day slow stochastic below 25 on SPY
ideas.entry: 7-day stochastic with 3-bar smoothing (slow %K) closes below 25. Headline test buys at that same close; realistic variant buys at the next open.
ideas.exit: Sell when price closes above yesterday's high (at that close; next open in the variant). No stop, no target, never more than one position.
ideas.claimed_results: 33 years of SPY. Close entry: 394 trades, 77.7% winners, profit factor 2.58, average trade 0.68% before costs. Next-open entry and exit: 394 trades, 73.6% winners, profit factor 2.47, average 0.65%. Lookbacks 4 to 12 all profitable with profit factor above 2.2. Alternative exits (stochastic above 50, 60 or 70; fixed 3 or 5 days) all profitable. Three eras: profit factor 2.66, 2.76, 2.23; last era 107 trades, 75.7% winners. Companion video: holdout 2016-2026 profit factor 1.75, median development grid profit factor 2.41. The oscillator-ranking video quotes 393 trades and 2.48 for the same setup.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Same family as the RSI(2) sweep (same exit); likely overlaps RSI(5) days.
ideas.red_flags: One market, in-sample, before commissions and slippage (the video says so). Close-entry headline is not executable exactly. Later era is weaker and holdout drops to 1.75. Shares an exit with every other idea in this family.
ideas.why_priority: Complete rules, a stated next-open result and parameter neighbourhood to reproduce; run in the same batch as A-03 because they are one family.

ideas.title: Perry Kaufman & Kevin Davey - Open Trading Questions & Answers
ideas.name: 200-bar price momentum as a regime filter instead of a 200-bar moving average
ideas.entry: Regime reading is the sign of today's close minus the close 200 bars ago; positive means momentum up. Davey says he does not treat this as permission to trade only long: some of his strategies short when momentum is up, and he tests both directions.
ideas.exit: unstated
ideas.claimed_results: No numbers. His stated reason: a 200-period moving average lags too much to serve as a regime filter, whereas the 200-bar change is quicker.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Direct companion to the 200 vs 222-day MA filter on SPY (P-0082). Same data, one extra column.
ideas.red_flags: Assertion without a test shown. A 200-day change and a 200-day average are strongly correlated, so a difference may be small and the risk of reading noise is high.
ideas.why_priority: Fully specified, trivial on free daily bars, and it extends a test we have already run.

ideas.name: ETH minus BTC relative-strength difference (CMMA)
ideas.markets: BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT hourly OHLC; BTC is the signal source, only ETH is traded
ideas.entry: cmma(x) = (close - SMA(24)) / (ATR(168) * sqrt(24)), ATR from pandas_ta on raw high/low/close, for both ETH and BTC. diff = cmma_ETH - cmma_BTC. Position in ETH only: long when diff goes above +0.25, short when it goes below -0.25
ideas.exit: Flat when diff returns to 0 or lower (long) or 0 or higher (short). No stop, no time stop
ideas.parameters: lookback 24, threshold 0.25, ATR lookback 168. Commented grid: lookback 6..72 step 3 x threshold 0.05..0.5 (19 values), scored by profit factor over the whole sample with no out-of-sample
ideas.claimed_results: none (README is empty; the script prints profit factor and per-side win rates only)
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead found: signal at bar i, return close i to i+1 (intermarket.py lines 104 and 119 in IntramarketDifference.txt). The function is called threshold_revert_signal but entry is momentum in relative strength (long the asset that is outperforming); only the exit is a reversion to zero. The grid is in-sample. The ETH leg is unhedged so crypto beta is in the returns. No costs. One pair on daily ETH-USD (starts late 2017, about 3,000 bars) is a small sample: test with the joint permutation of both series, and also run the rule on ETF pairs (sector ETF vs SPY) which have far more history. Lookbacks need rescaling for daily bars
ideas.why_priority: Complete rules and a cross-asset idea we have not tested, cheap on daily bars, and it forces us to build the joint-permutation test

ideas.name: Hawkes volatility compression-then-spike breakout
ideas.entry: norm_range = (ln high - ln low) / ATR(336), ATR computed on log high/low/close. Hawkes series h[t] = kappa * (h[t-1]*exp(-kappa) + norm_range[t]), kappa applied to the whole series at the end. Rolling 5th and 95th percentile of h over 168 bars (current bar included). last_below = most recent bar where h < q05. Entry on the bar where h crosses above q95 (h[t] > q95[t] and h[t-1] <= q95[t-1]) once a last_below exists: long if close[t] > close[last_below], else short
ideas.exit: Flat on the first bar where h < q05 again. No stop, no time stop; the position persists otherwise
ideas.parameters: kappa 0.1, norm ATR lookback 336, quantile lookback 168, quantiles 0.05 and 0.95. Commented grid: kappa [0.5, 0.25, 0.1, 0.05, 0.01] x quantile lookback [24, 48, 96, 168, 336] by profit factor, in-sample
ideas.claimed_results: none (README links a video; the script prints profit factor, win rates, average trade and time in market)
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead found: signal at close i, return close i to i+1 (hawkes.py line 132 in VolatilityHawkes.txt). The 5x5 grid is in-sample with no permutation test, so the 0.1/168 choice carries selection bias. Same-bar close fill, no costs. On daily bars the same bar counts mean a 336-day ATR and 168-day quantile window; trade count per market will be small, so run it on the 28-ETF set plus BTC and ETH
ideas.why_priority: Complete, look-ahead-free rules for a volatility regime idea that none of our current tests cover

ideas.title: Can Mean Reversion and Trend Following Work Together?
ideas.name: Weak-Monday reversal: Monday closes below the prior Friday's low, hold to Friday (also q6aVe5uOuH4)
ideas.entry: On a Monday, the close is below the previous Friday's low. In the combined strategy this leg also requires the close to be below the 200-day average. Entry price is not spoken; the Monday close is the likely reading. The transcript of this passage is garbled.
ideas.exit: Friday's close (the transcript adds a clause about the 200-day average that does not parse).
ideas.filters: close below 200-day average in the UYI0 version; none in the q6aVe5uOuH4 version
ideas.claimed_results: From q6aVe5uOuH4 (unfiltered, S&P 500, a strategy they sell): average gain 0.6% per trade, equal to about 7% a year, invested only 12% of the time; described as a pattern in which a weak Monday raises the odds of gains over the next four days to Friday's close. From UYI0 the bear-market leg is only quoted inside the 12% combined return (see A-14).
ideas.red_flags: Rules garbled and the sales version leaves 'weak' undefined. The numbers do not reconcile: 7% a year at 0.6% a trade is about 12 trades a year, and at a four-day hold that is about 19% exposure, not 12%, unless holds are shorter. No trade count, period or costs. Calendar effects are easy to overfit and the same channel found the Monday open-to-close effect to be noise (A-33).
ideas.why_priority: Cheap daily-only test of a calendar and reversal idea nothing in our set resembles, with a stated result, though the rule needs two readings pre-registered.

ideas.title: 6 Trading Ideas Most Traders Never Test - Kaufman & Davey
ideas.name: Trend-method ranking: breakout vs moving average vs regression vs exponential average, 80-day period (supported by FjqZttnWFQs)
ideas.entry: unstated beyond an 80-day calculation period; methods named are breakout, moving average, linear regression and exponential moving average
ideas.exit: unstated
ideas.claimed_results: Breakout does far better than every other trend method tested (teaser slide, figures not readable in the transcript) and few people use it. In the long Kaufman session he separately says the exponential average is the least effective of the trend methods, with breakout, plain moving average and linear regression all better.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Extends P-0084 (trend following on 28 ETFs). Add the four methods at the same 80-day length as extra arms, with Proteus pre-registering its own breakout and exit definitions.
ideas.red_flags: Teaser clip for a paid masterclass, rules and numbers withheld on purpose. The claim comes from one speaker's study on an unnamed market set.
ideas.why_priority: Cheap to bolt onto the queued trend portfolio and the claim is a ranking we can confirm or reject, but we would have to write the rules ourselves.

ideas.title: Improve Your Trading With Kaufman Indicators - Perry Kaufman And Kevin Davey
ideas.name: Kaufman adaptive moving average, with and without an efficiency-ratio gate, against a simple moving average
ideas.markets: Davey: E-mini S&P (360-minute bars) in the demo, then a wider basket; Kaufman: many futures and stocks
ideas.timeframe: intraday in Davey's test; Kaufman uses daily
ideas.entry: Davey's long-only test: buy when the close is above the average, sell when below; the simple-average baseline uses the same rule. Third arm: only buy when the efficiency ratio is above a threshold (threshold unstated). Kaufman's current settings: ER window 60 days instead of the original 10, and the fast end of the smoothing moved from about 2-3 days to 8; the slow end is unstated. He uses it as a plain trend follower, not a regime filter.
ideas.exit: Davey: close below the average. Kaufman: unstated beyond trend following.
ideas.filters: ER threshold (unstated), market selection by ER (see B-01)
ideas.claimed_results: On the ES example the adaptive average beat the simple one on profit, drawdown and return on account, and adding the ER gate improved a second example again. No figures given, single market and bar size. Kaufman says he has tested it over a broad range of markets and it beats moving averages.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Partial overlap with the 200 vs 222 MA test (it is a moving-average rule) and with P-0084 (trend arm).
ideas.red_flags: One-chart demo. Parameter settings differ between the two speakers. The Kaufman settings were chosen with hindsight on modern markets (he says the world changed after 2000).
ideas.why_priority: Concrete settings from the inventor and an easy comparison to a plain moving average, though the slow end and ER threshold are missing.

ideas.title: Algorithmic Trading Tools - Must Have!
ideas.name: Quit-rule menu applied to out-of-sample equity curves
ideas.entry: n/a (this decides when to stop trading a live strategy)
ideas.exit: Stop trading the strategy when a rule fires, measured from the start of out-of-sample or live trading. Rules named: last 12 months unprofitable; quit after 3 years of live performance (the best rule in one portfolio-level demo); a drawdown of 1.5 times the backtest maximum (the rule his own quitting behaviour matched). He says the tool carries 14 or 15 standard rules; the rest are unstated. No rule for restarting.
ideas.sizing: n/a. He insists on one rule for the whole portfolio, not a tuned rule per strategy.
ideas.claimed_results: Demo only, on strategies of unstated identity: one old strategy's out-of-sample began January 2012; the portfolio analyser (7 to 9 strategies) rated quitting after 3 years best. A separate quit game gave him 8.4 out of 10 on one strategy and showed he tends to give up at the second significant drawdown. No performance numbers.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Proteus already has a kill check (graduation G1 KILL) and week-8 pass marks; this would give a pre-registered menu of alternatives to compare.
ideas.red_flags: Tool is a paid-masterclass extra, not shown in detail. 'Quit after 3 years' as the best rule in a demo suggests strategies in the demo set decayed after development, which is a statement about those strategies, not a general result.
ideas.why_priority: We have several equity curves with a clear development/forward split and a kill rule is a real decision point; the three stated rules are enough to start.

ideas.title: I Let AI Build the Most Complicated Trading System Possible
ideas.name: Quarterly exam gate: sit in cash unless the strategy passed the past year
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures as tested; the gate itself is market independent
ideas.entry: Host strategy trades only in a quarter that follows a passed exam
ideas.exit: Host strategy exits as normal; if the exam is failed it sits out the next three months in cash
ideas.filters: Exam: prove yourself on the past year. The pass criterion (profit, Sharpe, anything else) is unstated.
ideas.claimed_results: 15 quarters, 2023 to 2026: it traded in 9 and failed its own exam in 6. It stayed out of April to June 2025, the tariff crash quarter, in which an ungated simple rule lost 28,560. Over the whole period the AI committee with all four changes (volatility-sized stops, same five entry times, trade only when expected profit clears a bar, quarterly exam) ended at +170 on 264 trades while the coin flip lost 179,805, the one-line rule lost 147,180 and buying every slot lost 85,390. Contribution of the exam alone is not separated from the other three changes.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Could be run as an overlay on the RSI(5) systems book and on P-0084
ideas.red_flags: Version two was run on history the author had already seen, so it is not blind. Only 264 trades; he says the uncertainty range includes zero. The exam alone is not isolated from three other changes. Equity-curve gating often just lags.
ideas.why_priority: A meta-rule we can test on daily strategies we already run, but it needs a pass criterion fixed in advance and the evidence in the video is thin.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Jobs-report fade held to the 9:30 cash open
ideas.entry: Jobs report is released at 8:30 New York. Wait five minutes, then trade against the direction of those five minutes. How the five-minute direction is measured (open to close of the window) is unstated.
ideas.exit: Hold until 9:30 when the regular stock market opens. Exits after 15 or 30 minutes lost in every variant tried.
ideas.filters: Jobs reports only. Does not work for inflation reports or Fed decisions.
ideas.sizing: one contract; two points of slippage per side plus commission (commission amount unstated)
ideas.claimed_results: 75 jobs reports: +22,795 (profitable in six of seven years and in both halves of the sample). Control: same trade at 8:30 on days with no release, drawn 10,000 times; median result -7,375; two of 10,000 baskets did as well. Double slippage (four points per side): +16,795. Eight points per side: +4,795. Waiting 1, 3, 10 or 15 minutes instead of five also works if the hold is about an hour. Author calls it a lead, not proof, and recommends a small forward test.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: 1-minute NQ (or ES) futures bars including the 8:30 to 9:30 pre-open session, 2020 onward (longer is better), plus verified jobs report dates. Not available from Yahoo daily bars. Video says its 10-market minute dataset cost about 75 dollars in total, vendor not named.
ideas.red_flags: Only 75 events. Found after asking many questions of the same data; the random-basket test does not correct for that, and the author says so. Fills at 8:35 on a data release can be much worse than the slippage assumed. 2022 is an outlier year for several results. Reason given for the reversal (thin liquidity before the cash open) is an interpretation he says he cannot prove.
ideas.why_priority: Complete rule, a proper luck control and a cost stress, but a small sample and no free data to test it.

ideas.title: I Tested Every Popular Day Trading Strategy. Your Favorite Is Dead.
ideas.name: Opening range breakout, 30 minute box, Nasdaq futures
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures (one NQ contract); also tested on nine other futures markets, gold was runner-up
ideas.entry: Wait 30 minutes after the 9:30 New York open, mark the high and low of that box. A close above the box is a buy, a close below is a sell. One trade a day. Bar size used for the close test is unstated.
ideas.exit: Stop on the opposite side of the box. Otherwise hold until the market closes. No target.
ideas.filters: none in the base version (see C-02 and C-03 for filters)
ideas.sizing: one contract; the micro Nasdaq contract (one tenth size) is suggested to shrink drawdown
ideas.claimed_results: Search: 10 futures markets, 1-minute bars 2020-2026 (6.6 million bars), nine famous strategies, a thousand settings, 3.58 million trades, 1,200 backtests, real commissions and slippage (amounts unstated). Settings chosen on 2020-2023, frozen, judged on 2024-2026. Nasdaq ORB total +96,825 on one contract over 2020-2026; positive in each year 2021 to 2025; about two thirds of its settings profitable on the unseen years; survived four times the slippage. Loses on about 52 percent of days. Normal days (two in three) lost 848,780, trend days made 945,605. Best 10 percent of trades made about nine times the total profit. Average win 2,208, average loss 1,891. About 89 percent of profit came from the long side; shorts roughly flat and losing in the last two years. 9 April 2025 alone +34,240. Worst drawdown 93,465 on NQ (9,410 on micro). Once lost seven months in a row and nine days in a row. 2026 year to date -59,555, and at recording it was 93,465 down since June. On gold, one extra tick of slippage turned it into a loser.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Intraday bars (1-minute ideal, 5-minute workable) for NQ or a Nasdaq proxy covering 2020-2026 with correct session times, plus a cost model. Yahoo gives no intraday history. Daily bars cannot place a 30 minute box.
ideas.red_flags: One survivor out of a thousand, on one market, in a mostly bull decade (author says so himself). Commission and slippage values are not given. Whole edge sits in rare trend days, so a short sample would mislead. Dollar results are for one contract with no percentage return. Author frames it as a candidate that still needs a forward test.
ideas.why_priority: The only strategy in this folder that survived a frozen out-of-sample judge and a cost stress, with near-complete rules, but we cannot test it without intraday data.

ideas.title: I Backtested 10 Oscillators on SPY for 33 Years
ideas.name: 7-day Chande Momentum Oscillator below -60 on SPY
ideas.entry: CMO over 7 days below -60 at the daily close; buy at the next open.
ideas.exit: Close above the previous day's high; exit at the next open.
ideas.claimed_results: 219 trades, profit factor 2.42, average trade 0.70%. Ranked fifth of ten. Described as having fewer trades and more variation across eras than the leaders; no era numbers given.

ideas.red_flags: Few trades, no robustness numbers given, selected from a ten-way ranking.

ideas.title: We Backtested Global Equities Momentum Across 55 Years
ideas.name: Antonacci global equities momentum (US versus non-US versus bills, monthly)

ideas.entry: At month end compute trailing 12-month returns. If US equities have not beaten Treasury bills, hold US aggregate bonds. Otherwise hold whichever of US or non-US equities has the higher 12-month return, for the next month.

ideas.title: Algorithmic Trading Tools - Must Have!
ideas.name: Equity-curve trading: take the next trade only when the strategy equity curve is above its 20-trade average
ideas.markets: any strategy's trade list (demo used a natural gas strategy)
ideas.entry: Take the next signal only if the strategy's own cumulative trade equity is above its 20-trade simple moving average. Mirror variant: turn off when the equity curve is making new highs.
ideas.exit: unstated; trades skipped while the curve is below the average
ideas.filters: 20-trade equity average (length is adjustable in his tool)

ideas.why_priority: Rule is complete and cheap, but the video's own demo says it did not work, so the value is a quick falsification.

ideas.name: Visibility-graph average path length long/short
ideas.entry: Take the last 12 raw closes (window ends at the current bar). Build a natural visibility graph of the window and of the negated window (ts2vg NaturalVG), compute the average shortest path length of each (networkx). Long (+1) if the price graph's path length is greater than the negated graph's, short (-1) if smaller, flat on a tie
ideas.exit: The position is re-decided every bar; no separate exit
ideas.parameters: lookback 12; commented heatmap lookback 6..24 by long, short and combined profit factor, in-sample. The graph is built on raw prices, not log prices, and visibility is not invariant to that choice
ideas.claimed_results: none
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead found: window ends at bar i, return is close i to i+1 (network_indicators.py lines 195 and 204). Odd mechanism with a 6..24 lookback sweep in-sample, so a pass needs a permutation test over the whole sweep. A 12-point visibility graph is trivial to write in numpy, so ts2vg and networkx are not required. Same-bar close fill
ideas.why_priority: One-line rule on a 12-bar window, almost free to run on 28 ETFs; the mechanism is odd so expect a null but it costs little

ideas.name: Market-profile support/resistance penetration
ideas.entry: Each bar: take the last 365 log closes (current included), fit a gaussian KDE (equal weights since first_w=1.0), evaluate on a 200-step grid between the window min and max, keep peaks whose prominence is at least 25% of the highest density as price levels. Long when close[t] > level and close[t-1] <= level; short when close[t] < level and close[t-1] >= level. If several levels cross on one bar the last in the list wins
ideas.exit: Reverse on the opposite cross; always in the market after the first signal. No stop
ideas.parameters: lookback 365, first_w 1.0, atr_mult 3.0, prominence threshold 0.25, KDE bandwidth factor = ATR(365, log) * 3. Nothing optimised in the code
ideas.claimed_results: none (the main block computes returns and trade lists but prints no statistics; comment calls it a trend following strategy)
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: none directly; it is a trend-following signal, related in family to P-0084
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead found: levels at bar i use closes up to bar i and the cross test compares close[i-1] with close[i] (mp_support_resist.py, TechnicalAnalysisAutomation.txt lines 1538-1565). The current close feeds the KDE that defines the level it then crosses. A scalar bw_method in scipy's gaussian_kde scales the window's standard deviation (line 1506), so kernel width is not ATR x 3 as the comment implies. No author results to compare against. Same-bar close fill. One KDE per bar makes permutation tests slow, so budget permutations
ideas.why_priority: Written on daily bars already so it runs as is on BTC, ETH and our ETFs with no rescaling, and the rules are complete

ideas.title: AI Created a Profitable SPY Strategy. Then We Tried to Break It

Costs: 10 basis points round trip gives 2.25, 20 gives 1.94. Weakest of four eras: 2010-2019 at 1.85. My arithmetic: $10,000 to $44,000 over about 33 years is roughly 4.6% a year.

ideas.title: Improve Your Trading With Kaufman Indicators - Perry Kaufman And Kevin Davey
ideas.name: Kaufman filter: a volatility band around the adaptive average to cut whipsaws
ideas.timeframe: intraday: bar sizes 180, then up to 1440 minutes (five sizes)
ideas.entry: Baseline: long when the average slopes up, short when it slopes down. Filtered version: enter only when the average has moved away from its latest turning point by more than a filter amount. Filter amount per Kaufman: one standard deviation of the average's movement over 10 to 15 days (the transcript is garbled on which series the deviation is taken of).
ideas.exit: unstated (presumably reversal of the slope, unconfirmed)
ideas.filters: band width one standard deviation; ER market selection suggested by Kaufman
ideas.claimed_results: 2007 to 2025, 44 markets, five bar sizes, walk-forward, any system with fewer than 50 trades dropped. The filter removed about 58 percent of trades (also described as roughly half). Average trade was still negative across all markets with the filter on, but less negative than off. Crude example: trades fell from 289 to 104, long and short sides both improved. A counter-trend (mean-reversion) version also lost trades without improving.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Davey used 180 to 1440-minute bars; a daily-bar version is a different test but the filter logic carries over.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Related to B-04 and P-0084; not previously tested.
ideas.red_flags: Davey says the aim is to compare filter on and off, not to trade the system, because it loses money overall. The filter definition is the weakest part of the transcript.
ideas.why_priority: Good evaluation design to copy (on/off over many markets, minimum 50 trades) but the filter formula is ambiguous.

ideas.title: Crude Oil AI Inspired Algo Trading Strategy - $96K in Walkforward Profits
ideas.name: Low-ADX short-term momentum in the direction of 200-bar momentum (crude oil)
ideas.markets: crude oil futures (CL continuous; a micro contract exists)
ideas.entry: Evaluated at the close of a bar, trade at the next bar's open. Long when ADX is below a threshold (period and threshold unstated), the close is above the previous close, the close one bar ago is above the close two bars ago, and the close is above the close 200 bars ago. Short is the mirror for the two close comparisons and the 200-bar test, with ADX still below the threshold.
ideas.exit: He mentions a couple of exits. Stated: a monthly cease-trading rule that switches the strategy off for the rest of the month after a profit or loss limit (limits unstated), and a catastrophic stop of 5,000 dollars (about 5 crude points). Anything else is in the book code, unstated.
ideas.claimed_results: Title says 96K of walk-forward profit (period unstated). About 60 to 61 percent winners, both long and short profitable at similar levels, largest loser about 6,800 dollars (larger than the 5,000 stop). Trade count fell sharply in the last 2 to 3 years, with long flat spells. Since the book release in early September 2025: one down month (November), a profitable December 2025 with 4 trades, good February and March 2026 with one trade.

Labelled AI inspired but nothing AI-specific is shown. Part of a book funnel; costs and slippage unstated. His own caveat: hard to trade alone because it sits out for long spells.

ideas.title: Perry Kaufman & Kevin Davey - Open Trading Questions & Answers
ideas.name: S&P moving-average length drift: long averages trend, short averages mean-revert, best now about 110 days (also in FjqZttnWFQs)
ideas.entry: Moving-average trend following with an optimised length; no crossover or filter detail given.
ideas.exit: unstated

Kaufman says the best S&P average length has crept up over decades (10, then 15, then 20 days) to about 110 days now, that on the S&P faster averages lose money while slow ones make money, and that in an optimisation the short end mean-reverts and the long end trends, though only modestly. He attributes it to higher volume bringing higher volatility after 2000.

ideas.title: Perry Kaufman & Kevin Davey - Open Trading Questions & Answers
ideas.name: Enter on the signal or wait for a pullback: waiting skips the winners
ideas.markets: any systematic entry (Davey: futures, Kaufman: stocks at the open)
ideas.timeframe: intraday execution; the claim can be proxied on daily bars
ideas.entry: Compare entering at the next open after a signal with placing a limit order for a better price and waiting. Pullback depth and waiting time unstated.
ideas.exit: unstated
ideas.claimed_results: No figures. Davey: entering on the signal matched the backtest and avoided regret. Kaufman: in the 1980s many traders waited for a pullback; the trades that did not pull back were the profitable ones, so waiting systematically misses winners and results get worse. Kaufman does allow a few minutes' wait and his own entries go in ahead of the open to avoid wide spreads.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Daily proxy: signal day close versus limit order a set percentage below, filled only if the next day's low reaches it. Fill modelling on daily bars is optimistic; true test needs intraday data.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Could be run on the RSI(5) ETF signals. Not tested before.
ideas.red_flags: Anecdote, not a test. Daily-bar limit fills overstate execution quality.

ideas.timeframe: unstated (lookback described as an important choice)
ideas.entry: Periodically re-rank markets by trailing trending-ness (ER or similar) and hold only the trending ones for a trend system; allow markets that were not trending to enter and drop ones that stopped.
ideas.exit: unstated
ideas.filters: ER rank with a lookback that is neither too long (you keep trading the same markets) nor so short it flips constantly; value unstated
ideas.sizing: equal risk per market (Kaufman: all positions at the same risk level)
ideas.claimed_results: None.
ideas.red_flags: No parameters. Selection by trailing performance-like measures can chase noise.

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: Jobs-report Friday weakness
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures as stated (daily proxies: QQQ, ^NDX)
ideas.entry: unstated (an observation, not a trade rule)
ideas.exit: unstated
ideas.filters: Jobs report days versus other Fridays without a release
ideas.claimed_results: On 74 jobs report days the Nasdaq returned -0.25 percent on average versus +0.06 percent on other Fridays; only 1.7 percent of random sets of ordinary Fridays were as weak. Negative in 2020, 2022, 2025 and 2026, positive in 2021, 2023 and 2024; fewer than half of jobs days were actually down, so a handful of big sell-offs drive the average. Author says it is not an edge.
ideas.red_flags: Tiny sample, average driven by a few days, return basis unstated, and the author himself labels it newsletter-grade seasonality. The jobs report date list is the awkward part because the statistics agency blocks automated downloads.
ideas.why_priority: Cheap to run on 25 plus years of daily data, and a good test of whether a post-2020 calendar quirk is just a short-sample accident.

ideas.name: Swing retracement ratios: do they cluster at 0.618 and 1.618
ideas.entry: Not a trading rule. Directional-change zigzag (a top confirmed when close falls sigma below the running high, a bottom when close rises sigma above the running low), leg ratio = |leg k| / |leg k-1|, kernel density of log(ratio) with bandwidth 0.01, plotted with vertical lines at 0.618 and 1.618
ideas.exit: unstated
ideas.parameters: sigma 1%, 2%, 3%, 4%; KDE bandwidth 0.01. The result is read by eye; the repo prints no statistic
ideas.claimed_results: none
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead issue because nothing is traded. The claim is unfalsifiable as written: we would need to define a density-mass test around 0.618 and 1.618 and compare it with permuted bars. Sigma needs rescaling for daily bars
ideas.why_priority: Cheap folklore test that tests the premise behind D-10 before we spend time on the harmonic strategy, and it makes a good public result either way

ideas.title: The Market Lies at 8:30 AM. I Tested 210 News Releases.
ideas.name: News-day switch: stand aside on Fed, inflation and jobs days for breakout strategies
ideas.markets: Nasdaq 100 futures; effect compared across the thousand-setting study on 10 futures markets
ideas.entry: Applies to a host strategy (the opening range breakout). Host entry as C-01.
ideas.exit: Applies to a host strategy; no separate exit
ideas.filters: No trade on the 210 event days: 52 Fed decisions, 80 inflation reports, 78 jobs reports since 2020
ideas.claimed_results: ORB lost 52,270 over about 200 news days and made roughly 149,095 on all other days (transcript text is garbled, but 96,825 plus 52,270 gives 149,095). Skipping news days lifts the total from 96,825 to about 149,095. Lost on news days in six of seven years; fewer than two in 100 random sets of 200 ordinary days were as bad. Across the thousand settings, mean-reversion types (VWAP fade, RSI, Bollinger reversal) did better on news days in 70 to 78 percent of settings; ORB and gap fill did worse on news days in 62 and 70 percent respectively (order as spoken).

The calendar part is free (Fed site dates; jobs and inflation dates need another route because the video says the statistics agency blocks automated downloads). A daily-bar version would be a different test: split our own RSI(5) trades by whether they straddle an event day.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: none directly; the daily analogue would act on the systems book (RSI(5) on nine ETFs)
ideas.red_flags: About 200 events, one host strategy, 2022 dominates several event results (author says so). Author notes his random-basket tests do not fully correct for how many questions he asked.

ideas.title: I Tested Every Popular Day Trading Strategy. Your Favorite Is Dead.
ideas.name: ORB version two: long side only, skip Mondays

ideas.exit: As C-01

Still loses money in more than four months out of ten. The Monday weakness showed up in both 2020-2023 and 2024-2026. ideas.name: Trendline breakout long/short (always in market)
ideas.markets: BTCUSDT hourly close (raw closes in trendline_breakout.py; log closes in the dataset and walk-forward files)
ideas.entry: Each bar, take the previous 72 closes (current bar excluded), fit an OLS line, then slide the slope by gradient search until it is the tightest line with every window close on one side: the resistance line pivots on the highest residual, the support line on the lowest. Project both to the current bar. Long if close > projected resistance, short if close < projected support
ideas.exit: Reverse on the opposite break; otherwise hold the previous signal
ideas.parameters: lookback 72; commented sweep 24..168 step 2 by profit factor, in-sample
ideas.claimed_results: none

Raw vs log price is inconsistent across files. The in-sample sweep has no permutation test. The pure-Python slope optimiser is slow per bar. Same-bar close fill

ideas.name: Trendline breakout with ATR barriers and random-forest meta-label
ideas.markets: BTCUSDT hourly OHLCV; scored from 2020 onward
ideas.entry: Resistance trendline on the previous 72 log closes as in D-06. Long at the close when close[t] > projected resistance and no trade is open. Features at entry: resistance slope / ATR, mean gap between line and window / ATR, max gap / ATR, volume / rolling 168-bar median volume, ADX(72). Label = trade return > 0. Walk-forward: RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=1000, max_depth=3, random_state=69420) trained on trades that both entered and exited inside the 2-year training window, retrained yearly; the trade is taken only if predicted probability > 0.5
ideas.exit: Take profit at entry + 3 ATR(168, log), stop at entry - 3 ATR, or 12 bars, checked on closes
ideas.parameters: lookback 72, hold 12, TP and SL multiples 3.0 and 3.0, ATR lookback 168, train 24*365*2, step 24*365, probability threshold 0.5. Nothing is optimised in the code
ideas.claimed_results: none (the script prints profit factor, average trade, win rate and time in market for all trades vs meta-labelled trades)
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Trade count is the limit: daily bars give far fewer entries than 8 years of hourly, so pool across the 28 ETFs with the ATR-normalised features
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Entry rule is in the P-0084 breakout family; the meta-label layer is new
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead found: training uses only trades with exit_i before the fit bar (walkforward.py line 519 in TrendlineBreakoutMetaLabel.txt) and features use bars up to the entry close. Long-only on a bull-heavy BTC sample; the repo compares against buy and hold but has no permutation test on the meta-labelled result. Same-bar close fill
ideas.why_priority: Meta-labelling is worth copying as a method, but this breakout rule yields few daily trades and overlaps P-0084

ideas.name: Walk-forward optimised Donchian close breakout
ideas.entry: upper = max of the previous (lookback-1) closes, lower = min of the same, both shifted one bar. Signal +1 if close > upper, -1 if close < lower, otherwise keep the previous signal
ideas.exit: Reverse on the opposite break; always in the market after the first signal
ideas.parameters: lookback optimised over 12..168 by profit factor on the training window (best on BTC 2016-2019 hourly was 19). Walk-forward: train 4 years of bars, re-optimise every 30 days of bars. Permutations: 1000 in-sample, 200 walk-forward
ideas.claimed_results: Code comment in donchian.py: best lookback 19, best in-sample profit factor 1.08 (BTC hourly 2016-2019). No p-values are written down anywhere
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: P-0084 100-day breakout (same family; here the lookback is optimised and it is a single market, long/short)
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead: the channel is shifted one bar and the walk-forward optimises only on bars before the fit date. The walk-forward test data ends in 2020 with a 4-year training window, so the out-of-sample stretch is about one year (walkforward_donchian_mcpt.py lines 431-436 in mcpt.txt). Same-bar close fill
ideas.why_priority: The strategy duplicates P-0084; the value is the walk-forward permutation method, listed under frameworks

ideas.name: Harmonic XABCD patterns (Gartley, Bat, Butterfly, Crab, Deep Crab, Cypher, Shark)
ideas.entry: Swings from directional_change at sigma. With X, A, B, C the last four confirmed swings and D the current bar's extreme (low if the last swing was a top, high if a bottom, and only if it is the most extreme since the last confirmed swing), compute XA/AB, AB/BC, BC/CD and XA/AD ratios and score them against hard-coded ratio ranges for the seven patterns (log-ratio error, out-of-range punished x2). Enter at the close of bar D when the best pattern error is at or below the threshold: long after a top-to-low leg, short after a bottom-to-high leg. Seven sigma values are run and the signals averaged
ideas.exit: Hold until the next swing is confirmed. No stop and no target
ideas.parameters: sigmas 1%, 1.5%, 2%, 2.5%, 3%, 3.5%, 4%; error threshold 0.5 in main (0.2 in the commented per-sigma tests; swept 0.1..0.75); ratio tables hard-coded. Sigma and threshold swept in-sample
ideas.claimed_results: none (a comment says profit factors above 4 are clipped on the chart because of low sample size)
ideas.red_flags: No strict look-ahead: swings are indexed by their confirmation bar. D is defined from the bar's own low or high, only known at that bar's close, so a fill at that close is optimistic. No stop. The scan stops at the last confirmed swing, so the final segment is dropped (harmonic_patterns.py line 778). Seven patterns x seven sigmas x threshold sweep is a big search space with no out-of-sample; a permutation test must put the whole family inside the loop. Sigma needs rescaling for daily bars
ideas.why_priority: Large untested search space and folklore premise; only worth running if D-09 finds real clustering at the Fibonacci ratios

ideas.name: Head and shoulders / inverse head and shoulders
ideas.entry: Rolling-window swings of half-width 'order' (a swing at bar t-order is confirmed at bar t). Five alternating swings: left shoulder, left armpit, head, right armpit, and a right shoulder defined as the highest close since the right armpit up to the previous bar. Rules: head above both shoulders; each shoulder above the midpoint of the other shoulder and its armpit; shoulder-to-head times within 2.5x of each other. Neckline through the two armpits. Short when close breaks below the neckline (early_find variant: when close falls below the midpoint of the right shoulder and right armpit). The inverse pattern is mirrored for longs
ideas.exit: Two versions coded: (a) hold for head_width bars (right armpit minus left armpit); (b) stop at the right-shoulder price, target = neckline value at entry -/+ head height, time stop at head_width bars, all checked on closes
ideas.parameters: order swept 1..48, early_find on and off; symmetry limit 2.5; no value selected in the code
ideas.claimed_results: none
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead found: rw_top and rw_bottom (TechnicalAnalysisAutomation.txt lines 2027-2054) confirm swings late and the code records the confirmation bar. Overlapping patterns and a 48-order x 4-variant sweep in test_hs_patterns.py mean the bar charts are not independent trades. Fills at the close. Pattern counts on daily bars will be small
ideas.why_priority: Classic pattern with fully coded rules, but low prior and a large unpenalised parameter sweep

ideas.name: Flags and pennants breakout
ideas.entry: Pole = move from a confirmed swing to the next opposite swing (rolling-window swings, half-width 'order'). Flag = the consolidation since the pole tip, valid if its width is at most half the pole width and its height is at most 0.75 of the pole height (0.5 in the PIP version). Trendline version: fit support and resistance lines to the flag so far and enter at the close of the first bar that closes beyond the line in the pole's direction (long after up-pole). PIP version: find 5 perceptually important points in the flag and require a zig-zag shape and a breakout beyond the flag line. A pennant is a flag with converging lines
ideas.exit: Hold for flag_width * 1.0 bars after the breakout bar
ideas.parameters: order swept 3..48; hold multiplier 1.0; two detectors (trendline and PIP) selectable
ideas.claimed_results: none
ideas.red_flags: No look-ahead found (flag fits use data up to the previous bar and the breakout is tested on the current close). Bugs: the pennant loops in flags_pennants.py use the stale variable flag.conf_x instead of pennant.conf_x (TechnicalAnalysisAutomation.txt lines 591 and 604; test_flag_patterns.py has it right), and lines 391 and 441 project the trendline one bar beyond the current bar. Overlapping patterns, order sweep with no out-of-sample
ideas.why_priority: Fully coded but low prior, a big sweep, and known bugs to fix before use

ideas.name: PIP shape miner with k-means clusters
ideas.markets: BTCUSDT hourly log close, 2018-2019 for the fit; walk-forward version on the full history
ideas.entry: Each bar, take the last 24 log closes, find 5 perceptually important points (vertical-distance method), z-score the 5 PIP prices and assign to the nearest of k k-means centres (k chosen by silhouette search over 5..40). Each cluster's past occurrences are scored by holding 6 bars; the single best cluster by Martin ratio (return over ulcer index) becomes the long cluster and the single worst the short cluster. Trade long when the current window falls in the long cluster, short when it falls in the short cluster
ideas.exit: Hold 6 bars; a new qualifying pattern resets the hold counter (wf_pip_miner.py)
ideas.parameters: n_pips 5, lookback 24, hold 6, clusters 5..40 via silhouette; walk-forward train 2 years of bars, retrain every 1 year
ideas.claimed_results: none (the permutation test that would give a p-value is commented out and 'takes about an hour' per 100 reps)
ideas.red_flags: Cluster selection (best and worst of k clusters, pip_pattern_miner.py lines 1917-1919) is done on the same data it is scored on, so the fit Martin ratio is selection-biased; the repo's own permutation test shuffles log returns and reruns the whole pipeline, which is the right cure. wf_pip_miner.py line 3007: the training slice always starts at bar 1, so the 'rolling' window actually expands. pyclustering needs numpy 1.23.1 (README); sklearn KMeans would replace it. No look-ahead found. Small sample on daily bars, and heavy compute

ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: EMA crossover overlaps the Davey golden cross we tested; RSI reversal overlaps the RSI(2) and RSI(5) tests. Those were intraday futures with costs, not daily ETFs.
ideas.red_flags: No rules or parameters, so nothing to replicate. The point is cost versus edge per trade on intraday data. The daily versions are not what he tested.
ideas.why_priority: A graveyard list with no rules; use it only as a reminder to compute edge per trade against cost per trade.

frameworks.name: Frozen development and holdout with an equal parameter budget
frameworks.what_it_is: Give each candidate the same number of parameter combinations (42 each), choose settings on 1993 to 2015, lock them, then judge only on an untouched 2016 to 2026 holdout. Use one common exit for all, switch no rules after seeing results, report the median profit factor over the whole grid as well as the winner, and score on fixed categories (profit factor, average trade, parameter robustness, drawdown, time robustness, trade count).
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: A template for pre-registering the week-8 review: same parameter budget per idea, a locked development window, a holdout nobody touches, and the grid median as a second pass mark beside the winner. Beware the lesson from this folder: a shortlist chosen from full-sample results contaminates the holdout.

frameworks.name: Neighbourhood robustness battery
frameworks.what_it_is: Do not trust the best cell. Sweep the main parameters, report the share of nearby settings with profit factor at least 2 and the median, require at least 100 trades before ranking, and keep the original pre-search rule rather than swapping in the search winner. Add: swap the exit across fixed 1, 3, 5, 10 and 21 day exits, split into eras, delay entry and exit to the next open, and stress costs at 10 and 20 basis points round trip (5yq3TpRpzuM and 7RUVOGEtAe0 run the same battery).
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add 'share of neighbours passing' and a cost-stress column to the systems book and to bin/review.py as a companion to the permutation test, which answers a different question (luck versus structure).

frameworks.name: Event study against same-horizon unconditional drift
frameworks.what_it_is: Turn a slogan into one frozen definition, use non-overlapping events, execute at the next open, and compare the conditional forward return with SPY's normal return over the same horizon, always quoting event count.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Run a drift-adjusted baseline for every new entry rule, including 'same exit from random entry days', so that exit-driven win rates are separated from entry edge. The close-above-yesterday's-high exit shared by most of these ideas needs exactly that control.

frameworks.name: Breadth over best-of: report the distribution across a universe
frameworks.what_it_is: Run one frozen rule across 101 stocks and report how many pass thresholds (above 1, above 1.5, above 2) and the median, rather than the top name, and re-run with next-open entry to show the realism cost.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Use the pass-share and median as the primary statistic for single-stock versions of the dip-buy, with a survivorship caveat written next to it.

frameworks.name: Layer low-exposure strategies and report exposure
frameworks.what_it_is: Dip-buying systems sit in the market about 12% of the time, leaving capital idle, so the proposal is to stack uncorrelated edges (trend, seasonal, other mean reversion). The combo video (UYI0piMbq2Q) shows a trend leg and a bear-market reversion leg switched by the 200-day average.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add an exposure percentage and a daily-P&L correlation matrix to the systems book so overlapping oscillator variants (A-03, A-04, A-07, A-22) are recognised as one edge, not four.

frameworks.name: Strategy factory pipeline: walk-forward, a marked live phase, and judge filters by on versus off
frameworks.what_it_is: Davey builds each strategy with walk-forward testing (optimise only on earlier data, then apply the result to unseen data), shows the closed-trade equity curve of the walk-forward results, then tracks a separate real-time phase from a fixed date (for example since a book was written in July 2025, or from 2021 for the portfolio strategies) with a dashed marker between development and live. His filter study used 44 markets, five bar sizes, 2007 to 2025, dropped any system with under 50 trades, and compared filter on versus off rather than looking at absolute profit. He also keeps one rule across a portfolio rather than tuning per strategy. Kaufman adds: test any change over 20 or more years, not the last few, and if a system trades rarely, extend the history and replicate on similar markets (corn on soybeans and wheat, one index on others).
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add a walk-forward harness to the probe loop, set an automatic 50-trade minimum, report every filter as an on-versus-off delta over the full 28-market set, and treat the commit timestamp as the start of the live phase. Note the caveat: a walk-forward curve is still developed data, so only post-commit results count as out-of-sample.

frameworks.name: Live versus ideal reconciliation and divergence alerts
frameworks.what_it_is: Plot the real account equity against the strategy engine's idealised equity on one chart. They drift because of missed, delayed or rejected orders, and he wants the real line at or above the ideal one. In another video he says he had AI write code that emails him when the strategy's number and the real number diverge. He also shows individual strategy curves next to the portfolio curve, and the losing months.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Extend audit/recompute.js so every night it compares the paper-trade ledger with an ideal signal replay and writes an alert line (and a Field Notes item) on divergence. Show the monthly return table including losing months on the lab page.

frameworks.name: Portfolio assembly: weekly correlation table, constant sizing, keep weak but uncorrelated strategies
frameworks.what_it_is: An equity curve combiner reads weekly returns of several strategies, draws the combined curve with a dashed line where out-of-sample starts, and prints a correlation matrix (his five demo strategies were near zero and two natural gas strategies were only about 0.1 apart). In the portfolio videos he covers six of seven futures sectors, trades one contract each so growth is not flattered by scaling size, and argues a strategy that loses money alone may still help by earning when the others lose.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Compute weekly return correlations across the nine-ETF RSI(5) book and the P-0084 portfolio, plot constant-unit curves, and test whether dropping the weakest standalone arm helps or hurts drawdown.

frameworks.name: Metric validation against forward results
frameworks.what_it_is: Do not discard a strategy because one metric looks bad (you can always find one) and do not borrow metrics from books. Pick the backtest metrics that you have shown correlate with later live performance. Davey says he did this over real-money history and found some metrics did not matter; he still uses net profit as his walk-forward objective despite the standard advice against it. No data is shown.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: With 80 or more probes, tabulate in-sample metrics (profit factor, win rate, drawdown, trade count) against forward outcome and pre-register which ones PASS-MARKS use. Treat his claim as unverified until our own table supports it.

frameworks.name: Where AI belongs and where it does not
frameworks.what_it_is: Fine uses: idea generation, feature ideas (turn off after a profit run), data cleaning (spotting decimal-point errors in highs), porting code between platforms, researching an economic rationale, analysing trade timing, writing monitoring scripts, and cross-auditing calculations with two different models. Not fine: letting AI set position sizing or risk limits, optimise parameters, run build and validation end to end, or design the portfolio. A specific trap: if AI finds a pattern or rationale on all your data and you then test on the same data, you have used the data twice.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Proteus is the case he warns about, so keep humans-in-charge items in code (pre-registered pass marks, permutation test, risk limits in CHARTER.md). Run a data sanity pass on Yahoo bars before each test, record which data the idea-finder saw, and have a second model recompute headline numbers.

frameworks.name: Quit rules and the quit game
frameworks.what_it_is: A library of standard rules for when to stop trading a strategy, replayed on out-of-sample curves, a portfolio version that picks one rule for all strategies, and an interactive game that reveals a hidden live curve step by step, asks you where you would quit, and scores that against the best risk-adjusted exit and the nearest standard rule. He found his own habit matched quitting at the second significant drawdown. He does not include restart rules, noting that it is psychologically hard to resume a strategy after it has just recovered.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: See B-05. The psychology half does not apply to an agent, but a pre-registered quit and restart rule per desk does.

frameworks.name: Fix the side and the sizing before seeing results
frameworks.what_it_is: Davey's ES strategy loses on the short side. His position: dropping the short side after seeing that is optimising by another route; decide long-only or long and short at the start. The same logic: do not pick the best position-sizing method per strategy, and do not assume a regime means longs only; test both sides.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Already close to Proteus practice. Make the direction and sizing choices explicit lines in every probe's pre-registration so they cannot be changed after the first result.

frameworks.name: Shadow log for discretion and know your engine's quirks
frameworks.what_it_is: If you want to override a system, log what you did next to what the system would have done and judge the override over time, including the mental cost. Both speakers say the best software is the one you know well enough to see how it can give false results, test daily systems on 1-minute bars when stops and limits are involved, and prefer uncleaned intraday data because live feeds contain bad ticks.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Keep a do-nothing shadow for any paper trade Luke or a child overrides. For daily tests, write down the fill assumptions (open, close, limit) in each probe note.

frameworks.name: Pre-committed plan for drawdowns
frameworks.what_it_is: In his contests Davey set up his plan to aim for 100 percent or blow the account. One year he started at 15,000 and was down about 50 percent after roughly three months, which was within the plan, and then months of nothing followed. Multiple 30 percent drawdowns and flat years happened even in the three winning years. His point is to prepare mentally for the worst case and keep to the plan.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: For the supercar target, write the acceptable drawdown and the stop line down before the first trade, with the sequence of long flat spells in mind.

frameworks.name: Freeze, then judge once; rank by the weaker period
frameworks.what_it_is: Search many configurations on a discovery window, require a minimum trade count, then rank survivors by the worse of the discovery and validation scores (so a strong period cannot hide a weak one). After choosing, freeze every parameter and run one forward block of fresh data with no new filter, stop or regime rule. If it fails, do not retune against that block, because it has become research data. Also show the frozen block separately from the full history, since the full curve can stay profitable while the frozen test fails. The same selected-then-frozen split (2020-2023 pick, 2024-2026 judge) is used in 8wJQrfn_otM and wed-hztsQlQ.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: For P-0084 and the RSI(5) systems book: choose parameters on one window, rank by the weaker of two sub-periods, write the frozen spec into the pre-registration commit, and report the judged block on its own line. Count the configurations searched in each P-number so the trial count is public.

frameworks.name: Same-trade random control baskets
frameworks.what_it_is: Run the identical trade (same clock time, same hold, same cost) on randomly chosen non-event days 10,000 times and report where the real result falls. Related versions: random entries with the same stop and target (200,000 trials, snZ89tkMFoA); a coin picks buy or sell at the system's own entry times 10,000 times, with every trade still paying its cost (wed-hztsQlQ); random sets of 200 ordinary days against the observed news-day loss.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Extend the permutation test used in P-0082: for each daily ETF strategy, draw random entry dates with matched holding period and exposure and report the share that beat the real result. For event-day ideas (C-05, C-06) draw random sets of ordinary days of the same size.

frameworks.name: Break-even win rate and the geometry check
frameworks.what_it_is: Before any backtest compute the win rate needed to break even, stop divided by stop plus target. A target five times closer than the stop hits first about five times in six whatever you do, so a high win rate is the starting line. Compare with random entries on the same bracket: if random does as well the signal is decoration. Check several brackets, not just the claimed one.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add break-even win rate and a same-bracket random-entry line to every report where a strategy has asymmetric stop and target or a limit exit (for example exits at yesterday's high). Treat any win rate above about 80 percent as a prompt to look for this.

frameworks.name: Pessimistic same-bar fill rule
frameworks.what_it_is: A bar gives open, high, low and close but not their order. When a bar touches both entry and target, or both stop and target, the optimistic assumption turns ambiguous bars into wins. Run both versions: optimistic, pessimistic (ambiguous counts as a loss) and a proven-wins-only count where the close is already beyond the target. Report the share of wins that come from ambiguous bars (65.7 percent in his test). The honest answer sits near the pessimistic one.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Daily bars have the same problem. Wherever a Proteus test uses a stop plus target, or fills at an intraday level such as a prior high, force the pessimistic order and report both. Add a switch to the shared backtest helper and log the gap between the two results.

frameworks.name: Cost stress and cost drag accounting
frameworks.what_it_is: Report edge per trade against cost per trade, and trades multiplied by cost (1,254 trades at 45 dollars was 56,430, more than a third of the whole loss in wed-hztsQlQ). Then stress: double or quadruple slippage and see whether the result survives; a one-tick change turned the runner-up on gold into a loser. In EruGJ-YIBWA doubling costs was one of four fragility checks, alongside nearby parameters, year-by-year splits and a frozen test.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: State the break-even round-trip cost in basis points for each ETF strategy and rerun at two and four times Proteus's assumed cost. Flag any rule whose edge per trade is below that.

frameworks.name: Profit concentration and decomposition
frameworks.what_it_is: Split results by day type (normal days versus trend days), side (89 percent of ORB profit from longs), year, month, and weekday. Report the share of profit from the best 10 percent of trades (nine times the total here), and the longest losing runs (seven months, nine days). Check whether any filter holds in both halves of the data; two of three filters flipped between periods.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add to the systems book report: top-decile trade share, long versus short split where relevant, worst month streak and a year table, so we can see whether a strategy is one fat tail in disguise and whether it would be survivable to run.

frameworks.name: Timing versus direction decomposition
frameworks.what_it_is: Take the exact moments a model chose to trade and swap its direction for a dumb rule; then run the dumb rule at all other moments. The model's direction made +170, the dumb rule at the model's moments made +10,900, the same rule elsewhere lost 155,655. Conclusion: the model knew when to stay out, not which way to go. Also sort trades by model confidence; the top 10 percent lost the most.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: For RSI(5) dip-buying, test whether the edge is in the entry timing (oversold days) or in being long at all: run the same dates with a plain buy-and-hold-for-N-days rule and the same exposure on non-signal days, and report each on its own line.

frameworks.name: Leak test by scrambling the future
frameworks.what_it_is: Deliberately scramble future data and check that none of the model inputs change; if a feature moves, it was peeking. Related: the pivot test in snZ89tkMFoA only lets a level trade after the right-hand confirmation bars have closed.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add a one-off test to every new signal function: shuffle all rows after bar t, recompute, and assert the signal at t is unchanged. Cheap insurance against lookahead in daily indicators.

frameworks.name: Event-study with a verified calendar and an event versus non-event control
frameworks.what_it_is: Build the event list from official sources, then verify each date against market behaviour (10-year Treasury futures volume about ten times normal in the first five minutes of a real release; this caught one wrong date, one holiday and several missing months). Exclude contract-roll days where they would distort a return. Measure events against random draws of ordinary days. Also note regime decay: reaction sizes differ by year, so an edge measured in 2022 may describe a market that has gone.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: For C-05 and C-06 build the Fed and jobs calendars once, check them against daily volume or range spikes in a Treasury ETF, and tabulate by year so a 2022-style outlier is visible.

frameworks.name: Rolling-window hot streak finder
frameworks.what_it_is: To see how a claim like 89 to 91 percent over 300 trades could arise, count the share of all possible 300-trade windows that reach the claimed rate (0.3 percent did), and which months they sit in. Also check the longest losing streak against the claim (five claimed, nine real).
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: When Proteus reads a claimed result from a short test window, compute how often a window of that length hits it in our own long daily history, and use the same to set expectations for the forward paper-trade of the RSI(5) book.

frameworks.name: Forward test compared with the backtest each week
frameworks.what_it_is: Treat a survivor of a thousand tests as a candidate. Trade it forward in small size and compare to the backtest every week; if behaviour drifts, assume the backtest was the liar. Choose position size so the worst drawdown is bearable (micro contract cuts drawdown from 93,465 to 9,410).
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Pre-register a divergence rule for the systems book: for example, a forward drawdown or hit rate outside a stated band of the backtest distribution for N weeks logs a kill or review line, decided before the first trade.

frameworks.name: Count the trials and state the limits
frameworks.what_it_is: Disclose that one survivor out of a thousand tests may be luck; that a Monday filter was found by looking at five weekdays; that random-basket tests do not fully correct for how many questions were asked; and that results rest on 39 to 208 events (LteukeidgbQ). Each video lists limits explicitly.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Keep a running trial counter in the track record (configurations searched, filters tried, weekdays or subperiods looked at) and print it beside each pass or fail, with a plain limits paragraph at the end of every probe write-up.

frameworks.name: Walk-forward permutation test
frameworks.what_it_is: walkforward_donchian_mcpt.py permutes only the bars after the training window (get_permutation with start_index = train window), then reruns the entire walk-forward, including the re-optimisation at every step, on each permuted series. The real walk-forward profit factor is ranked against 200 permuted ones, p = (1 + count of permuted results at least as good) / n. This tests the whole adaptive procedure out of sample, which the in-sample version cannot
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Apply to any rule with re-fitted parameters (D-01, D-08, anything with a sweep) and to a re-optimised version of the RSI(5) systems. Check that our numba bar_permute port supports start_index and keeps the pre-start bars real

frameworks.name: Joint multi-market permutation
frameworks.what_it_is: get_permutation accepts a list of OHLC frames and applies the same shuffle indices to every market (intrabar high/low/close offsets share one permutation, gaps share another), so cross-market correlation survives. The demo shows BTC/ETH correlation preserved. It asserts identical date indexes
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Needed for the 28-ETF portfolio in P-0084 (shuffling each ETF independently destroys the correlation structure and flatters diversified portfolios) and for pair or relative-strength rules such as D-02. Align the ETF dates first, which means the shortest history sets the sample

frameworks.name: Meta-labelling with purged walk-forward
frameworks.what_it_is: A primary rule generates trades with ATR take-profit, stop and time exit. A random forest (1000 trees, depth 3) is trained on past trades only (entered and exited before the fit date), refitted yearly, and a new trade is taken only if its predicted win probability exceeds 0.5. Compared with taking every trade and with buy and hold. Features are all ATR-normalised so they pool across assets
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Meta-label the RSI(5) dip-buying signals across the nine index ETFs (features: distance below the 200-day MA, ATR-normalised drop, volume ratio, prior-day return). Needs enough trades per training window, so pool markets. Needs its own permutation test, which the repo lacks

frameworks.name: Confirmation-index convention for swings
frameworks.what_it_is: Every swing high or low is stored with two indices: the bar where it occurred and the later bar where it became knowable (conf_index and the close at that bar). rw_top and directional_change do the same in TechnicalAnalysisAutomation. The sanity-check function asserts alternation and monotone indices
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Copy the convention into any pattern idea so entries use only confirmed swings and the look-ahead audit is mechanical

frameworks.name: Whole-pipeline permutation for clustering strategies
frameworks.what_it_is: pip_pattern_miner.py shuffles the close's log returns and reruns the entire fit (pattern extraction, silhouette k search, k-means, best and worst cluster selection) on each permutation, using the Martin ratio (return divided by ulcer index, sign-agnostic) as the score
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Template for testing any strategy whose parameters or clusters are chosen by search: the permutation loop must repeat the search, not just the final rule
